title: Decode a Multiplexed CAN Signal Group
statement:
A CAN frame has eight bytes and no room to waste, so signals that are
never relevant at the same time often share the same bit positions --
which one applies is decided by a **multiplexor**, a small field elsewhere
in the frame. Decoding a multiplexed message means reading the mux value
first, and only then knowing which of several completely different bit
layouts the rest of the payload has to be read as. Get the mux value wrong
and you do not get a wrong number back -- you get the *right kind of
question* asked of the *wrong bits*, silently.

This one combines two things earlier CAN exercises kept separate: unpacking
a little-endian (Intel byte order) multi-byte field, and sign-extending a
two's-complement bit field that is narrower than any C integer type.

## Your function

```
int32_t can_mux_decode(const uint8_t *frame, int32_t length,
                       int32_t *out_a, int32_t *out_b);
```

Byte 0's **low nibble** (bits 0-3) is the multiplexor; its high nibble is
reserved and carries no meaning. Depending on the multiplexor value:

- **mux 0** -- requires `length >= 5`.
  - `*out_a` = bytes 1-2 as an unsigned 16-bit value, **Intel (little-endian)
    byte order**: byte 1 is the low byte, byte 2 the high byte.
  - `*out_b` = bytes 3-4 as a little-endian 16-bit word, of which only the
    **low 12 bits** are the field; sign-extend those 12 bits to a full
    `int32_t` (two's complement, range -2048..2047). The top 4 bits of that
    16-bit word are unused padding and must be masked off, not included in
    either the value or the sign decision.
  - Return `0`.
- **mux 1** -- requires `length >= 3`.
  - `*out_a` = byte 1, read as a signed 8-bit two's-complement value,
    sign-extended to `int32_t` (range -128..127).
  - `*out_b` = bit 0 of byte 2 only (`0` or `1`); the other 7 bits of that
    byte are unused and must be masked off.
  - Return `1`.
- **any other multiplexor value (2-15), or `length` too short for the
  multiplexor that was selected** -- reject the frame: return `-1` and
  leave `*out_a` and `*out_b` untouched.

## Watch out

- **The multiplexor is the low nibble of byte 0, not the whole byte.** A
  byte 0 of `0x10` has multiplexor `0`, not `16` -- `0x10 & 0x0F == 0`. Code
  that switches on `frame[0]` directly instead of `frame[0] & 0x0F`
  correctly handles every frame where the high nibble happens to be zero and
  silently rejects every frame where it is not, for a reason that has
  nothing to do with the actual multiplexor value.
- **An unrecognised multiplexor must be rejected outright, even when the
  frame is otherwise a perfectly plausible length.** There is no fallback
  interpretation -- decoding unknown bits as if they were a known signal
  shape is exactly the failure mode a multiplexor exists to prevent, and a
  fixed test sends a full 8-byte frame with an out-of-range multiplexor to
  check that length alone does not make it acceptable.
- **Check `length` against what the *selected* multiplexor needs before
  reading that far into `frame`.** A short frame that happens to claim
  multiplexor 0 must be rejected on length grounds before any of bytes 3-4
  are touched, not read speculatively and rejected afterwards.
- The 12-bit field's sign bit is bit 11 of the 12-bit value (bit 3 of byte
  4), not bit 15 of the containing 16-bit word -- the padding bits above it
  are not part of the two's-complement representation at all.

tests.name: mux 0 unpacks a little-endian pair, ignoring byte 0's high nibble
tests.description: byte0 = 0xF0: low nibble is mux 0, high nibble 0xF is noise that must not affect the result.

tests.name: mux 0 sign-extends the 12-bit field at both boundaries
tests.description: Raw 12-bit values 0xFFF, 0x800 and 0x7FF are -1, the most negative value -2048, and the most positive value 2047 -- the padding nibble above each (0xA, 0x3, 0x3) must be masked off, not read as part of the value or the sign.

tests.name: mux 1 sign-extends an 8-bit value and masks the flag to bit 0
tests.description: 0x80 as a signed byte is -128; 0xFD's bit 0 is 1, its other bits are noise. 0x05 is positive; 0x02's bit 0 is 0.

tests.name: an unrecognised multiplexor is rejected even in a full-length frame
tests.stdin:
8
02 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF
4
0F 11 22 33
tests.description: mux 2 and mux 15 are both outside the recognised 0/1 range -- plenty of bytes present does not make an unknown multiplexor acceptable.

tests.name: a frame too short for its own multiplexor is rejected, not overread
tests.description: mux 0 needs 5 bytes and only has 3; mux 1 needs 3 and only has 2.
